newsitem.title: TAIWAN: CPC gives Taiwan final say on S.Africa project.
newsitem.headline: CPC gives Taiwan final say on S.Africa project.

text.p: Taiwan state oil monopoly Chinese Petroleum said on Friday it would defer to the Taiwan government when considering whether to continue its investment project in South Africa.
But company president Pan Wen-yen cautioned that economic considerations could not be given less weight than politics in evaluating such overseas investments.
"Whether or not we will continue our ongoing project in South Africa will depend on the (Taiwan) government's policy," Pan told reporters in Taipei.

Pan spoke two days after South Africa announced that it would sever diplomatic ties with Taipei in 1997 in favour of Beijing, triggering a review of Taiwan's investment policies toward South Africa and creating pressure on Taipei to reduce or withdraw its South African investments.
"But we cannot be expected to do money-losing business for the sake of complying with government policy," Pan added.
Pan's comment appeared to indicate that Chinese Petroleum was unwilling to walk away from a profitable project in South Africa merely for the sake of promoting government interests.
"We also have to consider economic efficiency," he said.

Pan said that Chinese Petroleum had put 12 of its 18 major overseas projects on hold, reflecting a policy first announced on October 24 to bolster state-sector investment in Taiwan to ensure a local economic recovery.
Pan stressed that the South African project was not among those frozen, making clear that the project would go forth unless Taiwan's government adopted a policy of halting it.

Pan was speaking at his first formal news conference since taking the reins of the huge oil monopoly on November 21, replacing Chen Kuo-young in a shakeup triggered by a spate of fires, explosions, leaks and other accidents.

Pan declined to give details of the South Africa investment, noting only that it was part of a family of projects based around a planned US$3.5 billion petrochemical project headed up by Taiwan's Tuntex Distinct Corp.
Tuntex itself said on Thursday it would respect the Taiwan government's wishes in deciding whether to continue the project.
Pan said that aside from the South African project, the six investments still under way included one each in Brunei, Malaysia, an unspecified Mideast country, Canada and the U.S. state of Alaska.
All remained in the evaluation stage, he said.
